title: Minimal degree of a Jacobian counterexample
W: The 2026 counterexamples to the Jacobian conjecture in three variables have degree 7 at best (Alpöge's map has component degrees 7,6,4). Wang's theorem says degree 2 is impossible. Find the smallest degree a three-variable counterexample can have: some number from 3 to 7.
M: Call $F=(F_1,F_2,F_3)\in\mathbb C[x,y,z]^3$ a Keller map if $\det JF\in\mathbb C^{\times}$, and set $\deg F=\max_i\deg F_i$. Determine $d_3=\min\{\deg F: F \text{ a Keller map that is not injective on }\mathbb C^3\}$. Known: $3\le d_3\le 7$ (Wang: degree $\le2$ Keller maps are invertible in every dimension; Alpöge, van den Essen: explicit degree-7 examples). In particular, is every cubic Keller map $\mathbb C^3\to\mathbb C^3$ invertible?
why: Now that the Jacobian conjecture is known to fail in dimension 3, the obvious next question is how small a failure can be. The minimal degree marks the line between low-degree regimes where invertibility can still be proved (Wang's degree-2 theorem, cubic-homogeneous results in small dimension) and the region where counterexamples exist. Because the Bass–Connell–Wright reduction raises the dimension, the cubic case in dimension 3 is a genuinely separate question.
issues: The original said 'the 2026 counterexamples have degree 7'. That is accurate for Alpöge's F (7,6,4) and van den Essen's (7,5,4), but Gallagher-type examples have higher degree, so I reworded it to 'degree 7 at best'. I defined 'Keller map' and 'degree' (max component degree, as opposed to geometric degree) and stated the known bounds 3<=d_3<=7. I found no paper that determines d_3 or settles the general cubic case in C^3, but the question is probably being actively studied. It is also a finite-dimensional algebraic problem for each degree, so computer searches may settle it soon, which lowers its long-term novelty.

title: Fluid in a box blows up
W: Show that a viscous fluid in a closed box with sticky walls can blow up in finite time under a smooth push.
M: Construct $u_0\in C_c^\infty((0,1)^3)$, divergence-free, and $f\in C^\infty([0,1]^3\times[0,T))$ such that the 3D Navier–Stokes solution in the unit cube with no-slip boundary condition becomes singular as $t\uparrow T$.
why: This would be the bounded-domain, no-slip version of the 2026 forced blow-up of Navier–Stokes. Since that blow-up can be localised, the bounded-domain version is a corollary, not a new problem.
issues: This is already known, and it is close to trivial. OpenAI's 2026 construction gives blow-up from zero data with a force in C_c^infty(R^3 x (0,inf)). Cao–Chi–Nie (arXiv 2609.10262, Cor. 3.14 and Prop. 3.16) glue such a blow-up into an interior ball of a bounded box or smooth domain with no-slip boundary, and Prop. 3.16 starts from zero initial velocity. More simply, cut off the stream function of the R^3 blow-up solution near the singular point. This gives a compactly supported, divergence-free velocity that blows up, and its Navier–Stokes residual is a force that is smooth on [0,T) and vanishes near the walls. As stated, the problem has no content beyond these results.

title: Unforced blow-up near the forced one
W: The 2026 forced Navier–Stokes blow-up uses a force that is smooth through the blow-up time. Can the force be made to vanish identically at the blow-up instant while staying smooth up to and including that instant?
M: Do there exist $T>0$ and $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3\times(0,\infty))$ with $f(\cdot,T)\equiv0$ such that the 3D Navier–Stokes solution on $\mathbb R^3$ with $u_0=0$ and force $f$ satisfies $\limsup_{t\uparrow T}\|u(t)\|_{L^\infty}=\infty$? (Requiring $f\equiv0$ on $[T-\delta,T]$ for some $\delta>0$ instead would be equivalent to unforced blow-up from smooth data, which is the Millennium problem.)
why: Requiring the force to vanish at the blow-up time is a small step from forced blow-up toward unforced blow-up. It tests whether the OpenAI construction really needs active forcing at the singular moment. The construction's force is already flat at the singular point, so this refinement asks whether the rest of the forcing can be switched off in time as well.
issues: As originally stated (f smooth only on [0,T), with ||f(t)||_{L^2}->0), the problem is close to routine. The OpenAI force is C_c^infty in space-time and vanishes to infinite order at the singular point. Set v=u+phi(t)h with h=-P f(.,T) and phi(T)=0, phi'(T)=1. The residual of v is then a force that is smooth on [0,T), and its L^2 norm tends to 0 if tau*||grad u(t)||_2 -> 0, which the self-similar scaling should give. So I tightened M to require f smooth through T with f(.,T)=0. Even that version is a technical variant of a known construction, and it does not approach the unforced problem.
